ety.text: Inherited from Middle English ande, from Old English anda (“grudge, enmity, malice, envy, hatred, anger, zeal, annoyance, vexation; zeal; injury, mischief; fear, horror”) and Old Norse andi (“breath, wind, spirit”); both from Proto-Germanic *anadô (“breath, anger, zeal”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₂enh₁- (“to breathe, blow”). Cognate with German Ahnd, And (“woe, grief”), Danish ånde (“breath”), Swedish anda, ande (“spirit, breath, wind, ingenuity, intellect”), Icelandic andi (“spirit”), Albanian ëndë (“pleasure, delight”), Latin animus (“spirit, soul”). Related to onde.

chain.g: to be envious or jealous, envy

ety.text: Inherited from Middle English anden, from Old English andian (“to be envious or jealous, envy”) and Old Norse anda (“to breathe”); both from Proto-Germanic *anadōną (“to breathe, sputter”). Cognate with German ahnden (“to avenge, punish”), Danish ånde (“to breathe”), Swedish andas (“to breathe”), Icelandic anda (“to breathe”). See above.

senses.d: Used simply to connect two noun phrases, adjectives or adverbs.
ex: Soupes dorye. — Take gode almaunde mylke […] caste þher-to Safroun an Salt […]
Sweet lady, you have given me life and living; […]

senses.d: Simply connecting two clauses or sentences.
ex: "Consensus is essential for the country," he said, adding that he was not "tied" to his post and was willing to step aside.

senses.d: Introducing a clause or sentence which follows on in time or consequence from the first.
ex: I'd been walking since sunrise, and I was hungry.

2007: Jimmy Carr, 8 out of 10 Cats, 13th day of July episode
Romance is dead; men killed it, and made women clean up the mess.
Hee said, I goe sir, and went not.

senses.d: Used to connect certain numbers: connecting units when they precede tens (now dated); connecting shillings to pence in a monetary quantity (now historical); connecting tens and units to hundreds, thousands etc. (now often omitted in US); to connect fractions to wholes.
ex: The One Hundred and One Dalmatians.
[H]e had bought the pen-holder during his last holidays at Blackstable for one and two-pence.

senses.d: Used to connect more than two elements together in a chain, sometimes to stress the number of elements.
ex: Lions, and tigers, and bears! Oh, my!
And these does she apply, for warnings and portents, / And euils imminent; and on her knee / Hath begg'd, that I will stay at home to day.

senses.d: Connecting two identical elements, with implications of continued or infinite repetition.
ex: I will extol thee, my God, O king; and I will bless thy name for ever and ever.
He was at work in a nearby city when the tsunami struck. ‘As soon as I saw it, I called home. It rang and rang, but there was no answer.’

senses.d: Introducing a parenthetical or explanatory clause.
ex: The word "capable" occurs in Mr. Fisher's Bill, and rightly, because our mental and physical capacities are infinitely varied.

senses.d: Introducing the continuation of narration from a previous understood point; also used alone as a question: ‘and so what?’.
ex: ‘And, Vera,’ added Mrs. Durmot, turning to her sixteen-year-old niece, ‘be careful what colour ribbon you wear in your hair[…].’

senses.d: Used to connect two verbs where the second is dependent on the first: ‘to’. Used especially after come, go and try.
ex: "What have you a been and given Pitt's wife?" said the individual in ribbons, when Pitt and Lady Jane had taken leave of the old gentleman.
Remember and help yourself to the soup! called Gavin.

senses.d: In rhythm, the second half of a divided beat.
ex: The same goes for measure 42, when you begin the phrase on the and of 1, because that kind of lick can easily bog down the time.

used at the end of a list to indicate the last item
